cards.text: The Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem, opened his book by saying, "Everything is futile!" (Eccl 1:2). Now he tells us how he got there. He was king over Israel in Jerusalem, and he set his mind to explore by wisdom all that is done under heaven.

cards.question: After exploring all that is done under heaven, how does the Teacher describe the task God has laid on people to keep them occupied?

cards.text: He's seen all the things that are done under the sun, and his verdict is "futile, a pursuit of the wind." Friend, that is NOT going on a motivational poster.

cards.question: The Teacher calls everything done under the sun a pursuit of the wind. What is that picture saying?

answers.text: Chasing what can never be caught
Running hard toward a sure prize
Sailing safely back to the shore

cards.text: Then he drops a short saying about crooked things and missing things. Real short. Real heavy.

cards.question: The Teacher says that what is crooked can be straightened.

cards.text: Then the Teacher has a little talk with himself. No judgment, friend: I give myself a pep talk before every batch, and I STILL burn the first tray.

cards.question: The Teacher tells himself he has grown in ___ beyond all those before him who were over Jerusalem.

cards.text: So he sets his mind to know wisdom, and madness and folly too. His conclusion? That line again: "this, too, is a pursuit of the wind."

cards.question: The Teacher explains why chasing wisdom didn't satisfy him. What does he say comes with much wisdom?
The Teacher says that as knowledge grows, grief shrinks.

cards.text: Next, the Teacher says to himself, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good!" Friend, that's me at midnight telling myself, just ONE more batch.

cards.question: The Teacher finds that pleasure gives him what wisdom couldn't.

cards.text: Then he turns to laughter. Now hold on, friend. This one's personal. Laughter is my WHOLE thing.

cards.question: What does the Teacher say about laughter?

cards.text: He even tries to cheer his body with wine and to embrace folly. Hold on, though. This is an EXPERIMENT, and the king is running it on himself.

cards.question: Even while he embraces folly, the Teacher's mind is still guiding him with ___.
What is the Teacher trying to find out with his experiment during the few days of people's lives?

answers.text: What is worthwhile for people to do
How long a king can stay in power
Which nation is the strongest of all

cards.text: So he expands his pursuits: houses, vineyards, and gardens and parks full of all kinds of fruit trees. This man didn't have a to-do list. He had a to-do SCROLL.

cards.question: To water his groves of flourishing trees, the Teacher built ___.

cards.text: Then he collects: servants, more herds and flocks than anyone in Jerusalem before him, silver and gold, the treasure of kings and provinces, even male and female singers. Meanwhile, I got bought out of a bakery bin for 25 cents.

cards.question: After becoming greater than everyone in Jerusalem before him, the Teacher says his wisdom stayed with him.
How much of what his eyes desired does the Teacher deny himself?

cards.text: His heart took delight in all his work, and that was the reward for all his labor. Then he steps back and considers everything his hands accomplished.

cards.question: Looking back on everything he toiled to achieve, what does the Teacher say there is to be gained under the sun?

cards.text: There it is again: "futile, a pursuit of the wind." He had EVERYTHING, friend, and the wind STILL won.

findings.problem: The card calls the Teacher 'the son of David, king in Jerusalem', which comes from Ecclesiastes 1:1. That verse is outside the passage, and the card gives no reference for it. Only the 1:2 quote gets a reference.

rule.text: Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'A rewarding task' could be argued from later in the passage. Ecclesiastes 2:10 says 'this was the reward for all my labor.'

rule.text: Each wrong answer must be false anywhere in the passage, not just at that moment.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'Then he drops a short saying about crooked things and missing things. Real short. Real heavy.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'So he sets his mind... His conclusion? That line again: ...'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The question says chasing wisdom 'didn't satisfy him.' The text never says that. It calls the search 'a pursuit of the wind' (Ecclesiastes 1:17).

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences: 'Then he turns to laughter. Now hold on, friend. This one's personal. Laughter is my WHOLE thing.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'He even tries... Hold on, though. This is an EXPERIMENT, and the king is running it on himself.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The right answer stands out. It is the only answer about people, and it echoes the question's 'people's lives.' The wrong answers, about a king staying in power and the strongest nation, have nothing to do with an experiment in wine and pleasure, so they aren't believable. The question also ties 'during the few days of people's lives' to the experiment. In Ecclesiastes 2:3, that phrase describes when people do what is worthwhile.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'So he expands his pursuits... This man didn't have a to-do list. He had a to-do SCROLL.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Reservoirs is one item in the Teacher's list of projects and possessions (Ecclesiastes 2:4-8). The baker doesn't need it to understand the passage, and it doesn't move the passage forward. The wrong answers, temples and towers, don't water trees, so the card is trivial. The list reads as a detail stretch, which belongs on one summary story card with no choice card.

rule.text: Ask about the moments that move the passage forward and the details the baker needs to understand it.
